scenario: A new batch job used the whole tokens-per-minute quota at lunchtime, and the shopping assistant returned errors for forty minutes.
options: Ask teams to run batch jobs at night
Route every app through an AI gateway with a token limit per consumer, and move the batch work to a Batch deployment
Buy more quota every time it happens
Give the assistant a larger model
explanation: Per-consumer token limits at the gateway stop one app starving another, and Batch deployments take bulk work off the live quota at half price. Asking nicely and buying quota reactively both leave the risk in place.

stem: Which change usually cuts the cost of a RAG assistant most without hurting quality, once proven by evaluation?
options: Raising the temperature
Sending all retrieved chunks rather than the top few
Routing simple questions to a small model, sending fewer and better-ranked chunks, and summarising older turns
Disabling content filters
explanation: Cost is calls × tokens × price, so cheaper models for easy questions and smaller inputs attack two of the terms directly. Evaluation confirms quality holds. More chunks raise cost, and filters do not affect price.

scenario: The team enables semantic caching at the gateway for all assistant traffic.
options: A shopper asking 'where is my order?' could receive another shopper's cached answer, or a stale one; cache only non-personal, non-time-sensitive answers
Caching increases token cost
Redis cannot store text
Cached answers bypass the model's context window
explanation: Semantically similar questions can need different answers when the answer depends on who is asking or when. FAQs such as the returns policy are safe to cache; order and account questions are not.

scenario: A security review finds the dev Foundry resource reachable from the internet with key-based access enabled. The team says it is only dev.
options: Leave dev open; only prod matters
Rotate the keys monthly
Put the keys in Key Vault and keep public access
Managed identities with local auth disabled and private endpoints in every environment, with Azure Policy denying resources that break it
explanation: Dev often holds real data and valid keys, and attackers do not care which environment it is. Policy makes the baseline automatic rather than dependent on review findings.

scenario: An email says a model version retires in 60 days. Nobody knows which apps use it.
stem: What practice would have made this routine?
options: Always use the newest model the day it launches
Never upgrade models
An inventory of deployments, models and versions in code, retirement dates tracked in the backlog, and the replacement evaluated against the test set well before the date
Let the deployment upgrade automatically and trust the new version
explanation: Retirement changes behaviour either way, so it needs the same evaluation as any other change. An inventory in Bicep answers 'who uses it', and early evaluation turns a deadline into a planned release.

scenario: Legal is writing the assistant's data-flow document and asks whether Microsoft could ever see prompts.
stem: What is accurate to tell them?
options: Prompts and outputs flagged as possible abuse can be retained for up to 30 days for review by authorised Microsoft staff, unless the organisation is approved for modified abuse monitoring
Microsoft uses all prompts to train future models
Nothing is ever stored anywhere
Prompts are shared with OpenAI for quality review
explanation: Azure does not train on your data or share it with OpenAI, but abuse monitoring is a real, documented exception that belongs in the data-flow document. Approved use cases can apply to change it.

stem: Why track cost per conversation, by app and feature, rather than the monthly AI bill?
options: Monthly bills are not available for AI services
It shows why cost changed and which lever to pull, and it scales with usage so growth is not mistaken for waste
It is required by Azure Policy
It avoids the need for budgets
explanation: A bigger monthly bill might mean success or waste. Cost per conversation, split by app through gateway metrics and tags, separates the two. Budgets and alerts are still needed on top.

scenario: The model provider has a regional incident and the assistant starts timing out.
stem: What should already be in place?
options: A support ticket template
A second assistant built on a different framework
Nothing; the assistant is not critical
A tested feature flag that falls back to plain search, plus gateway failover to another deployment or region where one exists
explanation: AI features need a graceful fallback, like any dependency. A tested kill switch keeps the shop usable, and gateway load balancing can route around a failing deployment before the switch is needed.
